Growing up outside a rural village in the north of Scotland, I learned early that the most useful skills are the ones nobody writes on a timetable. On Saturday mornings I worked the counter at a local grocer's shop, weighing vegetables, reckoning change in my head and listening to the regulars talk about weather, gaelic football and whatever had gone wrong in our local community that week. Those mornings taught me more about patience and about people than any classroom ever did.

When I was seventeen I started helping with a local food distribution initiative that ran out of a community centre twice a week. My job was mostly unglamorous: organising tables, organising food parcels, serving hot drinks for people who came in from the cold. Over time I found myself drawn to the quieter tables, where older men sat alone and wanted someone to listen. I came to understand that a good conversation can be as nourishing as the food, and that dignity is something you can either protect or quietly erode with a careless word.

These experiences shaped the question that now drives my interest in social policy. Why do some communities hold together through hardship while others fray? I have started to read about regional development, community governance and the economics of local business development, and I have noticed how often the answers depend on ordinary arrangements: who knows whom, who trusts whom, and who is willing to show up. I want to study this at a level where I can move from observation to evidence, and where I can test my assumptions against data and against the perspectives of people unlike myself.

I am aware that my experience is limited. I have not lived in a city, worked in a large institution or studied economics formally, and I expect that a university environment will challenge many of the conclusions I have drawn from one region of the country. That challenge is part of what attracts me. I want to be taught to doubt my own certainties and to build arguments that hold up beyond my own experience.

What I bring to a programme like this is a habit of paying attention: to the person at the counter, the one at the back of the hall, and data points on the page. I am eager to turn that habit into rigorous work, to collaborate with classmates who see the world differently, and to contribute to a community of learners who care about how societies treat their most vulnerable members. I believe this is where I can grow most, and where I can begin to give back what I have been given.

Dear Grandma Gloria,

I hope the garden is doing well and that your knees are behaving themselves this spring. Everything here in Vancouver is still grey and damp, but the maple outside our flat on Bathurst Street has started to bud, and I thought of you the moment I saw it. You always said the first leaves were a promise that winter was finished with us.

I finally sorted through the box you sent from Warsaw, and I found the photograph of you on the steps of the old tram depot, the one where you're holding the umbrella. I had the print framed and it now sits on my desk at work. My colleague Anna asked whether that was your hometown, and I said no, you were born in Gdańsk, but you grew up in Warsaw after the war. She thought that was a remarkable story, and so do I.

I have to tell you something practical as well. The consulate asked me to renew my passport, and I had to dig out my old national ID number, 84021733907, to fill in the forms. Grandma, you would have laughed at how long it took me to find it. Please don't worry, I have everything in order. On the twenty-second of April I'm booking the appointment, and I'll send you a photo of the new card the moment it arrives.

Give my love to Uncle Tadeusz and tell him the coffee in Vancouver is nothing like his.

With all my love,
Ewa
